Must know orientation
Antifolates exploit the difference between bacterial de novo folate synthesis and mammalian dietary folate uptake.
TMP–SMZ blocks two sequential folate steps. The lecture describes the combination as bactericidal synergy.
Fluoroquinolones trap DNA–enzyme cleavage complexes and cause lethal double-strand breaks.
Safety and stewardship are central themes in the later lecture sections.

XI • SULFONAMIDES & FOLATE

XI. Antifolate Drugs — A. Sulfonamide Overview

p. 16
  • Synthetic antibacterial agents that are primarily bacteriostatic when used alone.
  • Their mechanism centers on inhibition of bacterial folate synthesis.
    • Bacteria must manufacture their own folate.
    • Blocking folate synthesis prevents nucleotide production needed for growth and replication.
  • Classification by duration of action
    • Short-acting: sulfadiazine, 4–8 hours.
    • Intermediate: sulfamethoxazole, 8–12 hours.
    • Long-acting: sulfadoxine, approximately 7 days.
    • Other: mafenide and sulfacetamide.
  • Chemistry
    • Basic chemical entity: sulfanilamide.
    • N1 relates to antibacterial action.
    • N4 relates to pharmacokinetics and potency.
  • Lecture uses listed on p. 16
    • Urinary tract infection.
    • Upper and lower respiratory infections.
    • Bacterial diarrhea and dysentery.
    • Prevention of pneumonia.
    • Typhoid fever.
    • Prevention of infection on burned skin.

B. Folate Metabolism and Selective Toxicity

p. 16
  • Mammalian dietary import
    • Mammals lack the enzymes required for de novo folate synthesis.
    • Mammalian cells absorb preformed dietary folic acid or vitamin B9 using active transport proteins.
  • Bacterial transport deficit
    • Most pathogenic bacteria lack folate transport mechanisms and are impermeable to exogenous folic acid.
    • They must synthesize folates de novo from precursors including PABA.
  • THF function
    • Tetrahydrofolic acid serves as an essential carbon-donor coenzyme.
    • It is required for synthesis of thymidine, purines and methionine, supporting bacterial DNA, RNA and proteins.
Pteridine + PABA
substrates for early folate assembly
↓
DHPS
forms dihydrofolate pathway intermediates
↓
DHFR
forms tetrahydrofolate

Purines + thymidine

XI • MECHANISMS

C. Sulfonamide Mechanism of Action

pp. 16–17
  • PABA structural mimicry
    • Sulfonamides contain a para-aminobenzenesulfonamide core that resembles PABA.
  • Competitive DHPS blockade
    • They reversibly and competitively bind the DHPS active site.
    • PABA is prevented from participating in folate synthesis.
  • False substrate incorporation
    • DHPS can incorporate sulfonamide instead of PABA.
    • This produces a nonfunctional dead-end pteridine-sulfonamide conjugate.
  • Bacteriostatic arrest
    • Folate accumulation falls and cell division stops.
    • Existing cells are not actively killed by sulfonamide monotherapy.
  • Weak-acid behavior
    • Solubility decreases in acidic environments below pH 5.5.
    • Precipitation can produce crystalluria in acidic urine.

Sulfonamide Pharmacokinetics and Duration

p. 17
  • Modest tissue penetration with extensive plasma albumin binding. Albumin competition with bilirubin is emphasized.
  • Hepatic N-acetylation followed by renal excretion.
  • Sulfisoxazole: water-soluble, rapidly absorbed and excreted, useful for simple urinary infections.
  • Sulfamethoxazole: intermediate standard with about 10–12 hour half-life.
  • Sulfadoxine: ultra-long acting, used with pyrimethamine for malaria.

D. Trimethoprim Mechanism of Action

p. 17
  • Trimethoprim selectively blocks bacterial DHFR, preventing active THF formation.
  • Structural analogue
    • Resembles the pteridine portion of folic acid.
    • Binds reversibly and competitively to bacterial DHFR.
  • Enzymatic selectivity
    • Bacterial DHFR is described as 10,000 to 100,000 times more sensitive to trimethoprim inhibition than mammalian DHFR.
  • Weak-base distribution
    • Ion trapping produces high concentrations in acidic tissues.
    • The lecture highlights prostatic and vaginal fluid penetration.
  • Renal clearance
    • About 60–80% can be excreted unchanged in urine.
    • The plasma half-life is approximately 10–12 hours, aligning with sulfamethoxazole.
  • Pyrimethamine parallel
    • Related DHFR inhibitor with high affinity for protozoal DHFR, used for malaria and toxoplasma.

XI • BLOCKADE & RESISTANCE

E. Sequential Blockade

p. 17
  • Sequential blockade means two drugs inhibit consecutive enzymatic steps in the same metabolic pathway.
  • Transition to bactericidal power
    • Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim are individually bacteriostatic.
    • At the lecture’s 5:1 TMP–SMZ or co-trimoxazole ratio, sequential blockade shuts down two enzymes and is described as highly bactericidal.
  • Why resistance evolves more slowly
    • A bacterium must overcome more than one barrier in the pathway.
    • Clinical resistance to the combination develops more slowly than to either agent alone.
Sulfamethoxazole
blocks DHPS
↓
Reduced folate intermediate production
↓
Trimethoprim
blocks DHFR
↓
Loss of THF one-carbon donors
↓
Interrupted DNA assembly
bactericidal synergy
Important to know
First stop: sulfamethoxazole at DHPS.
Second stop: trimethoprim at DHFR.
Each drug alone is bacteriostatic. The fixed combination creates a double strike on the same pathway.
Lecture note: TMP–SMX is described as two hits on one folate pathway.

F. Antifolate Resistance

p. 17
  • Resistance may spread horizontally through plasmid-mediated genes.
  • Sulfonamide pathways
    • Mutated DHPS targets with reduced sulfonamide affinity.
    • Hyperproduction of PABA, sometimes up to 70-fold, outcompetes sulfonamide.
    • Porin changes or active multidrug efflux reduce intracellular drug accumulation.
  • Trimethoprim pathways
    • Plasmid-encoded modified DHFR with greatly reduced trimethoprim affinity.
    • Promoter mutations can overproduce normal DHFR, saturating the drug effect.
  • Cross-resistance reality
    • Plasmid-mediated transmission is common in Gram-negative bacilli such as E. coli.
    • The lecture reduces the pattern to four ideas: change the target, overwhelm the inhibitor, reduce intracellular drug concentration, and spread resistance genes.

XI • CLINICAL USE & TOXICITY

G. Antifolate Clinical Use

p. 18
  • Uncomplicated lower UTI
    • Empiric TMP–SMZ may be used for cystitis caused by E. coli, with local susceptibility screening because resistance is rising.
  • Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
    • TMP–SMZ is identified as the drug of choice for prevention and treatment in HIV/AIDS and other immunocompromised hosts.
  • Nocardiosis and toxoplasmosis
    • TMP–SMZ is drug of choice for systemic Nocardia.
    • Sulfadiazine with pyrimethamine is listed for Toxoplasma gondii brain abscesses.
  • Community-associated MRSA and Listeria backup
    • Oral backup for outpatient CA-MRSA skin infection.
    • Alternative for Listeria monocytogenes in penicillin-allergic patients.
  • Specialty topical or non-antibiotic uses
    • Sulfacetamide ophthalmic preparations for bacterial conjunctivitis.
    • Silver sulfadiazine and mafenide acetate for prevention or treatment of bacterial colonization in second- and third-degree burns.
    • Sulfasalazine is split by colonic bacteria into sulfapyridine and 5-aminosalicylic acid.

H. Antifolate Toxicity

p. 18
  • Sulfonamide hypersensitivity
    • Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are highlighted as the most feared reactions.
  • Crystalluria and hematuria
    • Precipitation in acidic urine can obstruct renal tubules.
    • Lecture prevention: high fluid intake and urine alkalinization.
  • G6PD deficiency
    • Oxidative red-cell stress can trigger hemolytic anemia.
  • Neonatal kernicterus
    • Sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin.
    • Late-pregnancy exposure is contraindicated in the lecture because free bilirubin can cross the newborn blood–brain barrier and deposit in basal ganglia.
  • Trimethoprim marrow toxicity
    • Folate deficiency may produce megaloblastic anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia.
    • Folinic acid or leucovorin is described as preventing or reversing hematotoxicity because bacterial cells cannot absorb it.
  • Hyperkalemia
    • Trimethoprim behaves as a weak potassium-sparing diuretic by blocking epithelial sodium channels in distal tubules.
  • AIDS sensitivity
    • The lecture states that up to 50–80% of AIDS patients given TMP–SMZ may develop severe adverse reactions including fever, rash, leukopenia, and diarrhea.
High-yield toxicity anchors
Sulfonamide: SJS or TEN, crystalluria, G6PD hemolysis, kernicterus.
Trimethoprim: megaloblastic change, hyperkalemia, high adverse-reaction burden in AIDS patients.

XII • FQ OVERVIEW & GENERATIONS

XII. Fluoroquinolones — A. Overview

p. 18
  • Semi-synthetic bactericidal agents that interfere with bacterial DNA metabolism.
  • Spectrum expands as newer agents are developed.
  • Nalidixic acid limitations
    • Lower potency.
    • High dose requirement.
    • Rapid resistance.
    • Less tissue and fluid penetration.
    • Use restricted to Gram-negative bacteria in the lecture overview.
  • Chemistry evolution
    • The lecture describes adding a fluoride ion and piperazine-related structural modifications to overcome older quinolone limitations.
    • Newer fluoroquinolones are more potent and penetrate tissues and fluids more effectively.

B. Fluoroquinolone Generations

Table 9. Fluoroquinolone Evolution
GenerationAgentsSpectrum or focusKey clinical uses
1stNalidixic acid, norfloxacinGram-negative aerobic bacilli. Norfloxacin has poor systemic bioavailability.Uncomplicated UTI only.
2ndCiprofloxacin, ofloxacinExpanded Gram-negative activity including Pseudomonas. Atypicals plus some Gram-positive cocci.Complicated UTI, prostatitis, infectious diarrhea, bone or joint infection, anthrax prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin.
3rdLevofloxacin, gemifloxacin, moxifloxacinStronger respiratory Gram-positive activity, especially pneumococcus. Atypicals.Community-acquired pneumonia and atypical pneumonia.
Advanced spectrumMoxifloxacin, delafloxacinStrong Gram-positive and atypical coverage plus anaerobes. Delafloxacin adds MRSA coverage.Intra-abdominal, pelvic, complicated skin and soft-tissue infections.
Key differentiator
Moxifloxacin is cleared through hepatic and biliary routes and does not achieve therapeutic urine concentrations.
Therefore, the lecture states that it is the only fluoroquinolone listed here that is not recommended for UTI.

XII • FQ MOA & PK

C. Mechanism of Action

p. 19
  • Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking transcription and replicated-chromosome separation.
  • DNA gyrase or topoisomerase II
    • Primary target emphasized for Gram-negative bacteria.
    • Introduces negative supercoils to offset positive supercoils created at replication forks.
    • Inhibition stops replication-fork progression.
  • Topoisomerase IV
    • Primary target emphasized for Gram-positive bacteria.
    • Separates linked circular daughter chromosomes after replication.
    • Inhibition blocks decatenation and cell division.
  • Lethal double-strand breaks
    • FQ freeze the enzyme–DNA complex mid-cleavage.
    • DNA remains broken, producing lethal genomic fragmentation.
  • Bactericidal dynamics
    • The class is described as highly bactericidal.
    • Like aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones show concentration-dependent killing and a post-antibiotic effect.
Lecture-specific internal inconsistency
The brief overview on p. 18 states DNA gyrase in Gram-positive bacteria and topoisomerase IV in Gram-negative bacteria.
The detailed mechanism on p. 19 and Appendix Figure 25 present DNA gyrase as the primary Gram-negative target and topoisomerase IV as the primary Gram-positive target.
This reviewer keeps both source statements visible and uses the detailed p. 19 relationship in the main mechanism layout rather than silently resolving the conflict.

D. Pharmacokinetics

p. 19
  • High oral bioavailability
    • Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin and moxifloxacin are cited at approximately 70–95% oral bioavailability.
    • This supports IV-to-oral transition.
  • Divalent and multivalent cation chelation
    • Antacids containing magnesium or aluminum, calcium, iron, sucralfate, and dairy can markedly reduce absorption.
    • The quinolone carboxylic-acid group forms insoluble complexes with metal ions, causing therapeutic failure.
  • Wide tissue penetration
    • High concentrations are achieved in bone, lung, prostate and phagocytic cells.
  • Renal secretion
    • Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin and ofloxacin are cleared primarily by glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion.
    • Probenecid blocks active tubular secretion and raises serum FQ levels.
  • Renal adjustment
    • Dose reductions are described as mandatory when creatinine clearance is <50 mL/min to prevent accumulation and CNS toxicity.
  • Moxifloxacin exception
    • Hepatic metabolism and biliary excretion.
    • No renal dose adjustment in the lecture.
    • Inadequate urinary concentrations, so not for UTI.

XII • FQ RESISTANCE & TOXICITY

E. Fluoroquinolone Resistance

pp. 19–20
  • QRDR point mutations
    • Resistance mutations cluster in the quinolone resistance-determining region.
    • gyrA is emphasized in Gram-negative bacteria.
    • parC is emphasized in Gram-positive bacteria.
    • A single amino-acid substitution can reduce fluoroquinolone binding affinity by 10–100 fold.
  • Gonococcal escape
    • Widespread empirical use selected rapid gyrA mutations in Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
    • The lecture notes that ceftriaxone replaced ciprofloxacin as standard therapy.
  • Efflux pumps
    • Transmembrane pumps in organisms such as S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, and M. tuberculosis actively extrude fluoroquinolones.
  • Porin loss
    • Gram-negative pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Serratia can down-regulate or delete porins such as OprD.
  • Plasmid-mediated Qnr
    • Qnr proteins protect DNA gyrase and add a transferable resistance layer.
    • Multiple mechanisms can accumulate and progressively increase resistance.

F. Toxicity

p. 20
  • Tendinitis and tendon rupture
    • Can be bilateral and frequently involves the Achilles tendon.
    • Lecture mechanism: magnesium chelation disrupts collagen synthesis and extracellular matrix integrity.
    • Higher risk with older age, renal failure, and concurrent corticosteroids.
  • Cartilage damage
    • Lecture contraindication: children under 18 and pregnant women unless no alternatives exist, such as anthrax or cystic fibrosis examples in the lecture.
  • Aortic aneurysm and dissection
    • The lecture states an FDA warning that risk may be doubled.
    • Avoid in high-risk cardiovascular patients.
  • QTc prolongation
    • Levofloxacin and moxifloxacin are highlighted.
    • Lecture contraindication with class IA or III antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone and sotalol.
  • CNS toxicity
    • Headache, dizziness, insomnia and occasional severe seizures are linked to interference with GABA binding.
    • Avoid in patients with pre-existing CNS lesions according to the lecture.
  • Dysglycemia
    • Gatifloxacin was withdrawn because of severe hypo- and hyperglycemia.
    • Current agents still carry warnings for glucose fluctuations in diabetes.
  • Phototoxicity
    • UVA exposure can trigger painful sunburn-like blistering.
    • The lecture advises avoiding direct sunlight during therapy.
Lecture safety emphasis
Cartilage damage, tendon rupture, QTc prolongation, and dysglycemias restrict class use.
Recognize serious adverse effects early and discontinue rather than continuing through toxicity.

H. Clinical Outlook — The Restraint Mandate

p. 20
  • Fluoroquinolones are potent broad-spectrum oral agents, but historical overuse has driven resistance.
  • The lecture emphasizes FDA safety alerts involving Achilles tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy and aortic dissection.
  • For minor infections such as bronchitis, sinusitis or uncomplicated UTI, the lecture favors a narrower agent when one will work.
  • Preserve for severe niches
    • Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia.
    • Complicated osteomyelitis.
    • Nosocomial pneumonia.
    • Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
  • Stewardship roadmap
    • Start narrow when appropriate.
    • De-escalate once susceptibilities are known.
    • Screen for advanced age over 60, CKD, corticosteroid use, G6PD status, and pre-existing QTc prolongation.
    • Actively monitor for Achilles tendon pain, severe sunlight sensitivity, or skin irritation.

XIII • HYPERSENSITIVITY

XIII. Common and Serious Adverse Effects — A. Hypersensitivity

p. 21
  • Immune-mediated responses range from mild skin rashes to severe anaphylaxis.
  • Reactions may be IgE-mediated or non-IgE mediated.
  • The lecture labels this section as a Type A or unpredictable reaction.
Lecture-specific labeling
Page 21 labels hypersensitivity as Type A or unpredictable. The organ-specific toxicity section is labeled Type B or predictable, and superinfection is also labeled Type B or predictable.
These labels are retained as written in the lecture and are not replaced with outside ADR classifications.
Table 10. Management of Antibiotic Hypersensitivity Reaction
ManagementDescription
Immediate discontinuationPromptly stop the suspected antibiotic.<br>For severe reactions such as anaphylaxis, stabilize airway, breathing and circulation.
Symptomatic reliefAntihistamines for mild cutaneous symptoms.<br>Corticosteroids may reduce inflammation.<br>Epinephrine is crucial for anaphylaxis and may be combined with IV fluids to stabilize blood pressure.
Patient education and documentationTeach the patient the specific antibiotic and reaction type.<br>Ensure visible documentation in the medical record to reduce medication error.

XIII • ORGAN TOXICITY & SUPERINFECTION

B. Organ-Specific Toxicities

p. 21
  • Direct toxicity can involve kidneys, liver, ears, nervous system, or hematologic system.
  • The lecture describes these reactions as usually dose dependent.
  • For serious reactions, discontinue, adjust the dose, or change the drug and seek an alternative.

C. Superinfection

pp. 21–22
  • Prolonged antibiotic use disrupts normal microbiota and can permit opportunistic secondary infection.
  • Risk factors
    • Course longer than 7 days.
    • Broad-spectrum agents.
    • Immunosuppression.
    • ICU admission or critical illness.
    • Indwelling devices.
    • Extremes of age.
    • Prior antibiotic exposure within 90 days.
  • Clostridioides difficile colitis
    • Most clinically significant antibiotic superinfection in the lecture.
    • Highest-risk agents listed: fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, broad-spectrum beta-lactams.
    • Prevention centers on restricting high-risk agents.
  • Fungal superinfection
    • Oral and vaginal candidiasis, with invasive disease in immunocompromised patients.
    • Commonly associated with broad-spectrum fluoroquinolones, carbapenems, and extended-spectrum penicillins.
  • Bacterial superinfection
    • Examples include MRSA, VRE, ESBL producers and CRE.
    • Prevention: antibiotic stewardship and timely de-escalation.

XIII • SPECIAL POPULATIONS & INTERACTIONS

Special Populations

p. 22
  • Pregnancy
    • Safe options listed for all trimesters: penicillins and most cephalosporins.
    • Avoid throughout pregnancy in the lecture: tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and aminoglycosides except when severe infection requires them.
  • Pediatrics
    • Tetracyclines under 8 years: enamel hypoplasia and permanent discoloration.
    • Fluoroquinolones under 18 years: arthropathy concern, reserved for serious infections without alternatives.
    • Sulfonamides in neonates: kernicterus from bilirubin displacement.
    • Chloramphenicol in neonates: gray baby syndrome from immature glucuronidation.

D. Clinically Significant Drug–Drug Interactions

p. 22
  • The lecture flags interactions as a major source of altered efficacy and safety.
  • High-risk antibiotics require clear indication, monitoring, and documentation.
  • The comprehensive-review section later highlights patterns such as QT stacking, CYP induction or inhibition, warfarin effects, and serotonin toxicity.

E. Antimicrobial Resistance

p. 22
  • The lecture states that development of bacterial resistance leads to treatment failure and increased morbidity and mortality.
  • Resistance may be viewed as predictable or unpredictable in this adverse-effect framework.
  • Later stewardship tables group major mechanisms into drug destruction, altered targets, reduced permeability, efflux, pathway bypass or overproduction, and biofilm or persister states.

Empiric, Definitive, and Prophylactic Therapy

p. 23
  • Empiric therapy: begins before organism confirmation and is based on syndrome, severity, risk factors, and local resistance.
  • Definitive therapy: culture-directed. Narrow spectrum, optimize dose and duration, and remove redundant agents.
  • Chemoprophylaxis: prevents a defined infection in a defined risk window. Timing and limited duration are essential.
  • Source control: drain abscesses, remove infected devices, debride necrotic tissue, and relieve obstruction. Drugs alone may fail.
Table 15. MIC, MBC, Breakpoint, and Zone Diameter
MeasureDefinitionInterpretation
MICLowest antimicrobial concentration preventing visible growth after standardized incubation.Compared with organism/drug breakpoints to classify susceptible, intermediate or resistant. MIC is not a universal potency ranking across drugs.
MBCLowest concentration that kills approximately 99.9% of the starting inoculum.Determined by subculture from non-growing tubes or wells. MBC:MIC ratio may suggest tolerance but is not routinely required.
BreakpointThreshold integrating MIC distributions, PK/PD, dosing and clinical outcome data.Species, drug, method and standards-body specific. Can change over time.
Zone diameterInhibition zone in disk diffusion.Translated by standardized tables. Not simply interchangeable with MIC.
Important correction
A lower MIC does not automatically mean one antibiotic is clinically superior to another. Compare that MIC with the drug’s breakpoint, achievable exposure, infection site, and dosing regimen.

Time-dependent: %fT > MICBeta-lactamsMaintain free concentration above MIC. Shorter intervals or prolonged or continuous infusion may improve target attainment in selected severe infections.
Concentration-dependent: Cmax/MICAminoglycosidesHigher peak relative to MIC improves killing. Extended-interval dosing uses the PAE and may reduce toxicity.
Exposure-dependent: fAUC/MICVancomycin, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, tetracyclinesOptimize total exposure over 24 hours while respecting toxicity. Vancomycin monitoring commonly focuses on AUC rather than trough alone.

Synergy, Antagonism, and Combination Therapy

p. 23
  • Synergy means the combined effect exceeds the expected additive effect.
  • Lecture examples include beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside in selected enterococcal infection and TMP–SMZ sequential folate blockade.
  • Reasons for combination therapy: urgent empiric breadth, polymicrobial infection, synergy, prevention of resistance in high-burden infection, and diseases requiring multidrug regimens such as tuberculosis.
  • Costs include additive toxicity, interactions, C. difficile risk, selection pressure, expense, and possible antagonism.
  • De-escalate when cultures and the clinical trajectory permit.

XIV • COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW II

Antimicrobial Stewardship Checklist

p. 23
  • Right indication: document suspected or confirmed infection.
  • Right sampling: obtain cultures before therapy when safe.
  • Right drug: use guideline and antibiogram information.
  • Right dose: optimize PK/PD and adjust for organ dysfunction.
  • Right route: switch IV to oral when stable and absorbable.
  • Right duration: use the shortest evidence-supported course.
  • Right review: antibiotic timeout at 48–72 hours.
  • Right prevention: vaccination, hand hygiene, isolation, and device care.
Table 19. Penicillins Characteristics
Table 19. Penicillins Characteristics
DomainHigh-yield review
MechanismB-Lactam ring acylates PBPS blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking.
EffectBactericidal. time-dependent.
SpectrumNatural: streptococci, susceptible meningococci, spirochetes.
Anti-staphylococcal: MSSA. Aminopenicillins: add enterococci and
selected gram-negatives. Antipseudomonal: broader
gram-negative activity.
Clinical
uses		Penicillin G/V for susceptible streptococci/syphilis. nafcillin/oxacillin
for MSSA. amoxicillin/ampicillin for susceptible
respiratory/enterococcal pathogens. piperacillin-tazobactam for

Penicillin G is acid-labile. penicillin V/amoxicillin are oral options.
Adjust many agents in renal dysfunction.
Major
adverse
effects		Hypersensitivity, rash, interstitial nephritis, diarrhea/C. difficile,

common with EBV.

only against susceptible enzymes.
📌Exam &
clinical
pearls		Do not label every rash as anaphylaxis. Clarify timing, symptoms
and severity, allergy delabeling improves care. Anti- staphylococcal
penicillins cover MSSA-not MRSA

Table 25. Aminoglycosides
Table 25. Aminoglycosides
DomainHigh-yield review
MechanismIrreversibly bind 30S inhibit initiation, cause mRNA misreading and

uses		Severe aerobic gram- negative infection as part of empiric/targeted

tration		Highly polar. poor oral absorption and poor CSF penetration. Renal

clinical
pearls		No anaerobic activity because uptake requires oxygen-dependent

Once-daily dosing exploits concentration killing and PAE.

Classic no-coverage reminders
Aminoglycosides: no anaerobes.
Aztreonam: no Gram-positive organisms or anaerobes.
Vancomycin, daptomycin, linezolid: no Gram-negative organisms.
Daptomycin: no pneumonia.
Ertapenem: no reliable Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, or Enterococcus.
Ceftriaxone, ceftaroline, moxifloxacin: no reliable Pseudomonas.
Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin: not for pyelonephritis or bacteremia.
Metronidazole: anaerobes and protozoa, not aerobes.

CRAM SHEET

Core Antifolate Mechanism

pp. 16–18
  • Bacteria make folate. Mammals import folate. That difference creates selective toxicity.
  • Sulfonamide
    • PABA analogue.
    • Competitive DHPS inhibitor.
    • Weak acid.
    • Bacteriostatic alone.
  • Trimethoprim
    • Competitive DHFR inhibitor.
    • Weak base with ion trapping.
    • Bacterial DHFR is described as 10,000–100,000 times more sensitive than mammalian DHFR.
    • Bacteriostatic alone.
  • TMP–SMZ
    • Sequential DHPS → DHFR blockade.
    • Lecture 5:1 fixed-ratio concept.
    • Bactericidal synergy.
    • Resistance develops more slowly than to either agent alone.
Antifolate red-flag toxicity
Sulfonamide: SJS or TEN, crystalluria, G6PD hemolysis, neonatal kernicterus.
Trimethoprim: megaloblastic anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hyperkalemia.
AIDS patients: lecture states 50–80% may develop severe TMP–SMZ adverse reactions.

Fluoroquinolone One-Minute Recall

pp. 18–20
  • DNA gyrase is emphasized as the main Gram-negative target.
  • Topoisomerase IV is emphasized as the main Gram-positive target.
  • Drug freezes the DNA–enzyme cleavage complex → double-strand DNA breaks → bactericidal effect.
  • High oral bioavailability, but metal cations chelate FQ and block absorption.
  • Cipro, levo, ofloxacin: mainly renal clearance.
  • Moxifloxacin: hepatic or biliary clearance, no renal adjustment in the lecture, and not for UTI.
  • Resistance: gyrA or parC mutations, efflux, porin loss, Qnr protection.
Fluoroquinolone must-know warnings
Tendon rupture or tendinitis, especially Achilles tendon.
Cartilage injury creates pediatric and pregnancy restrictions in the lecture.
Aortic aneurysm or dissection warning.
QTc prolongation, especially newer respiratory agents.
CNS toxicity, dysglycemia, and phototoxicity.
Stewardship message: preserve class power and use narrower agents when they will work.
Fast Drug Distinctions
DrugThinkDo not forget
TMP–SMZUTI, PJP, nocardiosis, CA-MRSA backupSJS or TEN, marrow effects, G6PD hemolysis, hyperkalemia
CiprofloxacinStrong Gram-negative, Pseudomonas, complicated UTI, diarrhea, anthraxCation chelation, renal clearance, tendon and CNS toxicity
LevofloxacinRespiratory FQ with Pseudomonas coverageRenal adjustment, QTc and dysglycemia
MoxifloxacinRespiratory + anaerobic coverageHepatic or biliary clearance. Not UTI. Highest QTc concern in lecture summary

Common Serious Antibiotic Adverse Effects

pp. 21–22
  • Hypersensitivity: stop suspected drug. Anaphylaxis requires epinephrine and ABC stabilization.
  • Nephrotoxicity: aminoglycosides and vancomycin are major anchors. Monitor creatinine and drug exposure.
  • Ototoxicity: aminoglycosides. Loop diuretics can amplify risk.
  • Hepatotoxicity: macrolides, TMP–SMZ, isoniazid and pyrazinamide are highlighted.
  • Neurotoxicity: fluoroquinolones and accumulated high-dose beta-lactams.
  • Hematologic toxicity: chloramphenicol aplasia, linezolid thrombocytopenia, sulfonamide G6PD hemolysis.
  • Superinfection: think C. difficile, Candida, and resistant organisms after broad or prolonged therapy.

Stewardship finish line
Right indication → right sample → right drug → right dose → right route → right duration → right review → right prevention.
The lecture’s antibiotic timeout is 48–72 hours.
